In Kananga, DRC, the Provincial Ministry of Justice of Kasai Central implemented
a randomized legal capacity building program at scale aimed at mediating
property, debt, and theft disputes between its citizens. This program has (i) a
“formal” legal capacity arm in which state lawyers serve as neighborhood legal
representatives and (ii) an “informal” legal capacity arm in which neighborhood
customary chiefs perform the same functions. We study how the program influences
dispute resolution and perceptions of the competence and impartiality of state
and customary systems. In turn, we investigate how these differentiated outcomes
shape property rights security, crime, violence, and tax compliance.
